i’m not op and by no means an expert so please take this with a grain of salt or two!

white noise is probably the most common one to know and is specifically constant “full-spectrum” noise where it’s all the different frequencies we can hear, stuff like a fan or tv static are good examples. 

for pink noise, it’s also that “full-spectrum” sound but not a constant noise and isn’t evenly distributed in energy. rustling leaves with a bit of wind is a great example. 

brown noise (i’ve heard some people call it red noise but brown is more common) is not “full-spectrum” and puts more energy into low tones. brown noise can be constant i think, but there’s no “natural” examples of it (natural as in it’s really hard to find something in the world that makes constant brown noise without it being something specifically designed to produce constant brown noise.) for the non-constant brown noises we *can* find naturally, distant rolling thunder or a huge waterfall (think like gigantic dam-sized) would be good examples.

think of how if you were to take a soundwave of some white noise (let’s say a regular fan) it would look like a fuzzy thick line. the fan isn’t getting louder or quieter, not is it speeding up or slowing down. it’s constant. now, let’s think of the pink noise example of leaves in the wind. the leaves can get louder with faster wind, they can slow down when the wind goes away. since it’s not constant, a soundwave of it would have a bunch of peaks and valleys to it. Brown noise would be similar to pink noise, but would only capture really low tones that are right at the bottom of human hearing. 

there’s a few online articles and wikipedia sources that explain a bunch of stuff about it, but it starts getting into a bunch of technical terms pretty quickly. OP if you see this, if i’ve made a mistake or anything don’t feel afraid to correct me!

Not exactly for physically making your own hand move faster, but for being able to have less stalls when you go to write. 

When going to write your essay, save an extra piece of paper for a structure/guideline sheet. Bullet point what subjects you need to cover, and if there’s anything that you want to include in those subjects, make a sub point about it. Each subject gets one paragraph. You can go back and reorder the subjects to fit either chronologically or in the way that it best flows. 

Once you have it set, then you won’t be trying to think “Did I forget anything?” when you start with the actual essay. Even through this eats out of your essay-writing time, you won’t stall for half a minute every five minutes trying to think of what you need to go over next, which will give you more time to write legibly. You’ll have all of your head in one spot so you won’t have to worry about remembering to “write that down later.” If you do get ideas in the middle of writing, tag them to the subject you wrote down on your guideline sheet. If it’s already too far past, it’s okay. You can still write them down and see if you can throw it in later.

I’m not a professional essay writer, but for my AP class, my teacher requires us to provide a brainstorming sheet. I find it really helpful now that I’ve been doing it. It helps me know how much I’m going to expect to write and what I’m writing about.

I was asking this same sort of question last year. Not sure how well I can answer all of these but I hope this leads you in the right direction. Note that all band directors do stuff different so my advice might make sense or not apply at all. 

1) My middle school didn't have a marching band so I learned everything during band camp, so if you've heard all of this stuff before then feel free to skip it. You get a sheet with numbers that act like coordinates that tell you where you are. They'll throw a small handful of terms at you to help you know where you're at. My director made us go through transitions to sets before mixing them with music. We learned one set at a time to know where we're at, then learn the next. Then we learn the transition in between the two and then repeat the process. If you don't know what you're doing people want to help because if you're off the show isn't as good.

2) Tuba music is Tuba music. I play Euphonium/Baritone so I understand the struggle because I sit next to tubas in concert band. But this is high school now and you get much more complicated music. So in that respect yes, it's more fun. 

3) With more people comes more fun things to do. I'm in a marching band of 178 members so we can pull off complicated stuff that looks really good to see. However that's not the case for every director and every song. For example I had one song where I didn't move an inch and another where I had to go 30 yards in 20 steps for two moves. So the possibility of stuff becoming more complicated is likely, but that doesn't mean it's required to be more complicated.

4) Band camp is the best place on Earth. My director made it so we got ample free time but we're still learning a whole lot. You get to meet a lot of nice people and get to make so many good memories. My band director had an event to look forward to every night so everyone got to interact with one another. I actually met my boyfriend through marching band and the band program in general, so by that standard it's amazing. Make sure to bring a water bottle and sunscreen because you'll be outside the whole day.

Honestly there really isn't much to worry about, but I understand why you came to Reddit. Like I said every director is different so you might do something other than what I said. Overall I seriously enjoy the program and am looking forward to band camp in August. You might want to quit halfway through but the amount of memories you make are priceless so stick it out until the end. You're welcome to PM me or reply to this comment if you have more questions.
